Case 4:25-cv-02588-HSG            Document 54        Filed 07/14/25      Page 1 of 3




                                   1

                                   2

                                   3

                                   4                                  UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   5                                 NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   6

                                   7     RANDALL WRIGHT,                                     Case No. 25-cv-02588-HSG
                                   8                    Plaintiff,                           ORDER DENYING MOTION FOR
                                                                                             APPOINTMENT OF INTERIM CLASS
                                   9              v.                                         COUNSEL
                                  10     SMART ERP SOLUTIONS, INC.,                          Re: Dkt. No. 34
                                  11                    Defendant.

                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          Before the Court is Plaintiffs’ application to appoint interim class counsel. See Dkt. No.

                                  14   34. Plaintiffs seek to appoint three attorneys from three different law firms as interim class

                                  15   counsel: (1) Jeff Ostrow of Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A.; (2) Scott Edward Cole of Cole & Van Note;

                                  16   and (3) John J. Nelson of Milberg Coleman Bryson Philips Grossman, PLLC. The motion is

                                  17   unopposed. Id. The Court held a hearing on this matter on July 10, 2025. Dkt. No. 53. The

                                  18   Court DENIES the motion.

                                  19          Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(g)(3), a court “may designate interim counsel to

                                  20   act on behalf of a putative class before determining whether to certify the action as a class action.”

                                  21   Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(g)(3). The rule “authorizes [a] court to designate interim counsel during the

                                  22   pre-certification period if necessary to protect the interests of the putative class.” See Fed. R. Civ.

                                  23   P. 23 (advisory committee’s notes to 2003 amendment); see also Manual for Complex Litig.,

                                  24   § 21.11 (4th ed. 2004) (“[D]esignation of interim counsel clarifies responsibility for protecting the

                                  25   interests of the class during precertification activities, such as making and responding to motions,

                                  26   conducting any necessary discovery, moving for class certification, and negotiating settlement.”).

                                  27   “Although Rule 23(g)(3) does not provide a standard for appointment of interim counsel, courts

                                  28   typically look to the factors used in determining the adequacy of class counsel under Rule
                                         Case 4:25-cv-02588-HSG            Document 54         Filed 07/14/25     Page 2 of 3




                                   1   23(g)(1)(A).” See, e.g., In re Seagate Tech. LLC Litig., No. 16-CV-00523-RMW, 2016 WL

                                   2   3401989, at *2 (N.D. Cal. June 21, 2016). These factors are:

                                   3
                                                      (1) the work counsel has done in identifying or investigating potential
                                   4                  claims in the action;
                                                      (2) counsel’s experience in handling class actions, other complex
                                   5                  litigation, and the types of claims asserted in the action;
                                                      (3) counsel’s knowledge of the applicable law; and
                                   6                  (4) the resources that counsel will commit to representing the class.
                                   7

                                   8   Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(g)(1)(A). The Court may also consider “any other matter pertinent to counsel’s

                                   9   ability to fairly and adequately represent the interests of the class.” See Fed. R. Civ. P.

                                  10   23(g)(1)(B).

                                  11          Here, counsel address the four factors under Rule 23(g)(1)(A), but fail to explain, as a

                                  12   threshold matter, why the appointment of interim counsel is necessary at this stage to protect the
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   interests of the putative class. “Where there are no competing lawsuits or firms, courts in this

                                  14   district have been unwilling to appoint interim class counsel.” See In re Seagate, 2016 WL

                                  15   3401989 (collecting cases). To date, counsel have all worked together cooperatively and appear to

                                  16   share a unified strategy regarding how this action should proceed. Moreover, the appointment of

                                  17   interim counsel is not necessary to address any live conflict among counsel or to clarify their
                                       respective roles in the litigation. See, e.g., Imran v. Vital Pharm., Inc., No. 18-CV-05758-JST,
                                  18
                                       2019 WL 1509180, at *10 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 5, 2019) (denying appointment of three firms as co-
                                  19
                                       interim class counsel where there was no rivalry among the firms).
                                  20
                                              At the motion hearing, counsel maintained that the appointment of interim counsel would
                                  21
                                       prevent duplicative effort by the attorneys and firms participating in this case. However, counsel
                                  22
                                       did not identify any live dispute or competing strategy among Plaintiffs’ counsel. As such,
                                  23
                                       counsel failed to concretely explain why they cannot coordinate tasks among themselves in a way
                                  24
                                       that avoids duplicative work—as they appear have been doing thus far—without the appointment
                                  25
                                       of interim counsel. Under the circumstances, it would be premature to appoint interim lead
                                  26
                                       counsel where the risk of internal conflict or future related cases being filed is speculative, and the
                                  27
                                       proposed benefit to the class is therefore unclear.
                                  28
                                                                                          2
                                         Case 4:25-cv-02588-HSG             Document 54        Filed 07/14/25     Page 3 of 3




                                   1            In short, the Court finds that counsel did “not present the ‘special circumstances’ that

                                   2   warrant appointment of interim counsel at this stage.” See In re Nissan N. Am., Inc. Litig., No. 18-

                                   3   CV-07292-HSG, 2019 WL 4601557, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 23, 2019) (quoting In re Nest Labs

                                   4   Litig., No. 14-CV-01363-BLF, 2014 WL 12878556, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 18, 2014)).

                                   5   Accordingly, the Court DENIES the motion without prejudice, Dkt. No. 34.

                                   6            Per the Court’s previous order, Plaintiffs’ consolidated complaint is due within 45 days of

                                   7   this Order. See Dkt. No. 29 at 3. Within 10 days after the consolidated complaint is filed, the

                                   8   parties shall submit an agreed upon briefing schedule to the Court for motion to dismiss briefing

                                   9   or the filing of an answer to the consolidated complaint.

                                  10

                                  11            IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                  12   Dated:     7/14/2025
Northern District of California
 United States District Court

                                                                                         HAYWOOD S. GILLIAM, JR.
                                  14                                                     United States District Judge
